name: Belmont-Paul Women's Equality National Monument
author: author-C-2026-10-18
summary:
A few blocks from the U.S. Capitol, at 144 Constitution Avenue NE, stands a brick federal-period house that the Park Service counts among the oldest residences in Washington, on land the Nacotchtank, or Anacostans, used for hunting and trading. Robert Sewall built the first house here in 1800, and Treasury Secretary Albert Gallatin rented it from 1801 to 1813. On August 24, 1814, British troops burned it after, by Sewall’s later claim to Congress, Commodore Joshua Barney’s men, retreating from the Battle of Bladensburg, fired on them from inside; the house standing today was rebuilt on the spot by 1820. [1]

In 1929 the National Woman’s Party, founded by Alice Paul in 1916–17, bought the house from Senator Porter Dale with the help of its president and benefactor Alva Belmont, and made it the party’s fifth and final headquarters. From here, the 2017 foundation document says, the party targeted more than 600 discriminatory laws and won more than 300 legislative changes — in marriage, divorce and custody law, jury service, property rights and contracts, the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 and the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Paul helped lead the party from the house until she retired in 1972. [2] [3]

The party fought to save the house when construction of the Hart Senate Office Building threatened it in the 1960s; it was listed on the National Register in 1972 and named a National Historic Landmark in 1974. On April 12, 2016, after the party donated the property, President Barack Obama designated it a national monument. [1] [3]

women.html:
On January 10, 1917, twelve party members began a silent vigil at the White House gates — reportedly the first people ever to picket it. After the United States entered World War I that April, spectators attacked the pickets; in June police began arresting them for obstructing traffic, and in July sixteen were sentenced to 60 days in Virginia’s Occoquan Workhouse. Officials abused the prisoners and held them in solitary confinement, the 2021 resource study records. Alice Paul, sentenced in October to seven months, the longest term, and Rose Winslow went on hunger strike and were force-fed. Publicity roused sympathy; the pickets were released in late November and their sentences invalidated in March 1918. [3]

The party then pursued an Equal Rights Amendment, drafted by its officers and lawyers after 1921 and rewritten by Paul in 1943. Introduced in every session of Congress from 1923, it passed in 1972 but was three states short of ratification at the 1982 deadline. [3]

black.html: For the March 3, 1913, suffrage parade on the eve of Woodrow Wilson’s inauguration, Paul, fearing she would alienate southern white women, tried to segregate Black marchers in a section at the rear; the 2021 resource study says it is unclear whether any actually marched there. The NAACP’s journal The Crisis counted about 40 Black women in the march, among them 25 Howard University students; Ida B. Wells-Barnett, reportedly told she could not march with the white Illinois delegation, waited at the side until the Chicago delegation passed, then stepped into the line with it. The study quotes historian Mary Walton’s judgment that Paul’s failure to welcome Black marchers left a permanent stain on her reputation. Mary Church Terrell marched in 1913 and later joined the White House pickets, while remaining critical of white suffragists’ disinterest in issues that mattered to Black women. [3]
